title: The Mathematics of Money
intro: Almost every model in finance is built from one idea: a sum of money today is worth more than the same sum later, because today's money can be invested to earn a return. This page builds compounding, present value, annuities, inflation and averaging of returns from that idea.

blocks.text: Simple and compound interest

With simple interest you earn the rate only on the original sum: \$1,000 at 5% earns \$50 every year. With compound interest each year's interest is added to the balance and itself earns interest. After $n$ years at rate $r$ a sum $PV$ grows to

\$1,000 at 5% for 30 years becomes $1000 \times 1.05^{30} \approx \$4{,}322$ compounded, against \$2,500 with simple interest. The gap is the interest on the interest, and it grows with time: the later years add far more than the early ones.
Compounding frequency and continuous compounding
If interest is paid $m$ times a year at a quoted annual rate $r$, each period earns $r/m$:

The effective annual rate (EAR, or APY for savings accounts in the US) is what you really earn in a year: $EAR = (1 + r/m)^m - 1$. A 12% rate compounded monthly is $1.01^{12} - 1 \approx 12.68\%$ effective. Loans quote an APR that is usually the nominal rate, so the true cost of a credit card at 24% APR compounded monthly is about 26.8%. Continuous compounding, $e^{r}$, is the limit and is what option models use because it makes the algebra clean.
The rule of 72

Money doubles in about $72 / r$ years, with $r$ in percent: at 6% about 12 years, at 9% about 8 years, at 2% about 36 years. The exact answer is $\ln 2 / \ln(1 + r)$; 72 is used because it has many divisors and is accurate for rates between about 4% and 12%. The same rule works for inflation: at 3% inflation prices double, and money's buying power halves, in about 24 years.

Present value and discounting
Turn the growth formula around and you get the value today of a sum due later. A payment $CF$ in $n$ years, at a discount rate $r$, is worth

The discount rate is the return you could earn elsewhere on an investment of similar risk: your opportunity cost. A riskier payment gets a higher discount rate, so it is worth less today. This one line is the root of bond pricing, stock valuation and almost every capital budgeting decision.
For a stream of cash flows you discount each one and add them up. The net present value of a project subtracts what it costs today:

A positive NPV means the investment earns more than the discount rate. The internal rate of return (IRR) is the rate that makes NPV zero; it is a bond's yield to maturity under another name. IRR has traps: a project with cash flows that change sign more than once can have several IRRs, and comparing IRRs of projects of different size or length can pick the wrong one. When they disagree, trust NPV.
Annuities and perpetuities
An annuity pays the same amount $C$ every period for $n$ periods: a mortgage, a bond's coupons, a pension. Its present value has a closed form:

A perpetuity pays forever, and its value is simply $C / r$. If the payment grows at rate $g$ each period (a growing perpetuity), it is worth $C_1 / (r - g)$ for $r > g$, where $C_1$ is next period's payment. That is the Gordon growth model for stocks on the Valuation page.
The future value of saving $C$ at the end of each period is $C\,[(1 + r)^n - 1] / r$. The plot above uses it with monthly periods.
Loans and mortgages
Solve the annuity formula for $C$ and you have a loan payment. A \$300,000 mortgage at 6% a year over 30 years has monthly rate $i = 0.005$ and $n = 360$ payments:

Over the life of the loan you pay about \$647,500, so \$347,500 is interest. Early payments are mostly interest; the share going to principal grows over time (this schedule is called amortization). Paying extra principal early saves the most interest.
Inflation and real returns

Inflation is the rise in the general price level, usually measured by a consumer price index (CPI). A nominal return is what you see on your statement; a real return is what you gain in buying power. The exact link is the Fisher equation:

A savings account at 4% with inflation at 3% earns about 1% real. Taxes make it worse: tax is charged on the nominal return, so at a 25% tax rate the after-tax nominal return is 3% and the real return is about 0%. Long-run real returns are what matter for planning: US stocks have returned roughly 6 to 7% a year above inflation over the last century, government bonds roughly 1 to 3%, and cash close to 0 to 1%, with long stretches far from those averages.
Measuring returns

The holding period return of an asset bought at $P_0$, sold at $P_1$, paying income $D$ along the way, is $(P_1 - P_0 + D)/P_0$. Total return counts the income (dividends, coupons) as well as the price change; a price chart without dividends understates stock returns by a lot over decades.
Arithmetic and geometric averages

Suppose a fund gains 50% one year and loses 50% the next. The arithmetic mean return is 0%, but \$100 becomes \$150 and then \$75: you lost 25%. The geometric mean, or compound annual growth rate (CAGR), tells the truth about growth:

Here CAGR $= \sqrt{1.5 \times 0.5} - 1 \approx -13.4\%$ a year. The geometric mean is always at or below the arithmetic mean, and the gap grows with volatility: approximately $g \approx \mu - \sigma^2/2$. This volatility drag is why a steadier investment with the same average return ends up with more money, and why losses hurt more than equal gains help: after a 50% loss you need a 100% gain to get back.

widget.title: Volatility drag: compound growth falls as volatility rises

blocks.text: The arithmetic mean is the right number for forecasting next year's expected return; the geometric mean is the right number for describing what happened over many years and for projecting long-run wealth. Fund marketing sometimes quotes the higher arithmetic figure.
Time-weighted and money-weighted returns

If you add or withdraw money, there are two ways to measure performance. The time-weighted return chains the returns of each sub-period and ignores the size of the flows: it measures the manager or the fund, and is what funds report. The money-weighted return is the IRR of your actual cash flows: it measures your experience, including whether you added money at good or bad times. Studies of fund investors (the Morningstar 'Mind the Gap' series, for example) regularly find that investors' money-weighted returns trail the funds' time-weighted returns by around a percentage point a year, because money flows in after good runs and out after bad ones.
Practice

blocks.title: Doubling time
blocks.text: How long does money take to double at 8% a year compounded yearly? Compare the rule of 72 with the exact answer.
solution: Exact: $n = \ln 2 / \ln 1.08 = 0.6931 / 0.07696 \approx 9.01$ years. The rule is almost exact here.

blocks.title: Present value of a promise
blocks.text: Someone offers you \$10,000 in 5 years. If you can earn 6% a year on similar-risk investments, what is the promise worth today?
solution: $PV = 10000 / 1.06^5 = 10000 / 1.3382 \approx \$7{,}473$. Paying more than that today would earn you less than 6%.

blocks.title: A growing perpetuity
blocks.text: A fund promises a payment of \$400 next year, growing 2% a year forever. At a discount rate of 6%, what is it worth?

blocks.title: Real return
blocks.text: Your bond fund returned 5.5% last year while inflation was 3.2%. What was your real return, exactly and approximately?
solution: Approximate: $5.5 - 3.2 = 2.3\%$. The approximation is close when rates are low.

blocks.title: The average that lies
blocks.text: A stock returns +30%, −20%, +25% and −10% in four years. What are its arithmetic mean and its CAGR?
blocks.hint: Multiply the growth factors $(1 + r_t)$, then take the fourth root.
solution: Growth: $1.3 \times 0.8 \times 1.25 \times 0.9 = 1.17$, so CAGR $= 1.17^{1/4} - 1 \approx 4.0\%$. The volatility costs over 2 points a year.

blocks.title: Saving for 30 years
blocks.text: You save \$500 a month for 30 years at 7% a year (compounded monthly). Roughly how much do you have? How much would a 1% yearly fee cost you?
solution: At 6%: $500 \times (1.005^{360} - 1)/0.005 \approx 500 \times 1004.5 \approx \$502{,}000$. The fee costs about \$108,000, nearly 18% of the result, though the fees themselves look small each year.
